name: autogen

facts.description: A programming framework for agentic AI

title: AutoGen: A Python Framework for Agentic AI Workflows
answer: AutoGen is a Python programming framework for agentic AI, created by Microsoft, that lets you build applications where multiple LLM-backed agents converse, use tools, and execute code to solve tasks. It sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack, above raw model APIs and below your application. The one thing to know before adopting it: AutoGen is powerful for multi-agent experimentation and production monitoring, but its API changed significantly at version 0.4, so you must choose a version and follow the migration guide.

sections.body: AutoGen is a programming framework for agentic AI, made by Microsoft and hosted at github.com/microsoft/autogen under the CC-BY-4.0 licence. It is written in Python and its repository shows active development into 2026. It appeared publicly by 2023, with a 0.2 documentation line and a 0.4 release noted on the official site. It occupies the orchestration layer of the AI stack: it does not train models or serve them at scale, but coordinates LLM calls, tool use, code execution, and multi-agent conversations on top of model APIs such as OpenAI or compatible endpoints.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework is used for multi-agent conversation patterns, enhanced LLM inference, and research prototypes. Its documentation describes MathChat, a conversational framework that pairs an LLM assistant with a user proxy agent to solve advanced mathematics, improving accuracy by about 6 percent overall and 15 percent in algebra over basic prompting. It also documents AutoDefense, a multi-agent jailbreak defense that filters harmful responses using one to three LLM agents. Enhanced inference features include caching, error handling, multi-config inference, result filtering, and templating. It is strongest when a task benefits from several specialized agents collaborating, or when you need to experiment with agent roles and prompts.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: AutoGen assumes comfort with Python and with calling LLM APIs. You configure agents through an llm_config argument containing a config_list of model dictionaries, and you need to understand concepts such as API keys, base URLs, and rate limits. The official site offers a migration guide from 0.2 to 0.4, blog posts with worked examples, and documentation pages on LLM configuration and enhanced inference. It does not present itself as a beginner's introduction to Python or to machine learning mathematics. A developer new to agents can start from the blog examples, but should expect to read configuration and API documentation carefully.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The project has a large community, with more than 61,000 stars on GitHub. The official site states it is the official project and is not affiliated with any forks or startups. It integrates with OpenAI and compatible endpoints, Azure OpenAI, and local models served through FastChat, including ChatGLM2-6B. It has a partnership with AgentOps as its official agent observability tool, requiring an AGENTOPS_API_KEY and a call to agentops.init(). Documentation covers LLM configuration, enhanced inference, and use cases, and the blog carries research and LLM-tagged posts. The site does not list every third-party integration.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: AutoGen supports both quick experiments and more controlled deployment. For prototyping, you can define agents and a config_list in a few lines and run multi-agent conversations, with caching and templating reducing repeated cost. For production, the documentation emphasizes observability through AgentOps, including monitoring of LLM calls, costs, latency, agent failures, multi-agent interactions, and tool usage, and it notes that enterprises can trust AutoGen in production with that monitoring. The cost of this flexibility is configuration complexity: model selection, retries across config_list entries, and deepcopy constraints on llm_config all require attention. The site does not claim that AutoGen itself provides high-throughput serving.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: AutoGen is a current, actively developed framework rather than a legacy choice, with a 0.4 release and a migration guide on the official site. Its adoption is visible in research prototypes such as MathChat and AutoDefense, and in enterprise monitoring through AgentOps. The site states that enterprises can now trust AutoGen in production with detailed monitoring and logging. For someone choosing what to learn, this suggests value in understanding multi-agent orchestration patterns, but the facts do not include named corporate users or job market data, so claims about specific employers or roles would go beyond what is supported.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: AutoGen is a Python framework, so it is typically used alongside Python data and ML libraries, and it calls LLMs through OpenAI-compatible APIs. The documentation shows it working with openai-python, with autogen.OpenAIWrapper for openai>=1, and with autogen.Completion as a drop-in replacement for openai.Completion and openai.ChatCompletion when using openai<1. It can point at local models through FastChat, which provides OpenAI-compatible APIs, and at Azure OpenAI. This places it in the polyglot pattern where Python orchestrates agents while model serving and observability are handled by separate tools such as FastChat and AgentOps.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The documentation shows several limits. AutoGen 0.4 introduced breaking changes, so older 0.2 examples may not run without migration. Model selection inside a config_list is not intelligent by default: an agent uses the first available model and retries others only on failure, and the site says there is generally no hidden logic to pick the best model, though some specialized agents may try. Deepcopy of llm_config can fail for objects without a __deepcopy__ method. The site does not state benchmark performance against other agent frameworks, does not list all supported model providers, and does not give a complete production hardening guide.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
